matches.abstract_excerpt: Standard weight decay treats each weight matrix as a vector and ignores its spectral structure. We introduce spectral weight decay, a post-step decoupled nuclear-norm update that applies additive rather than multiplicative spectral shrinkage. passages.text: Training Arabic large language models faces challenges from noisy web data, dialectal variation, and the high cost of continual pretraining (CPT). We introduce AQL-Lite (AQL: Arabic Quality Language ), a time- and resource-efficient framework for adapting a multilingual LLM to Modern Standard Arabic (MSA). AQL-Lite couples a quality-first curation pipeline (structural cleaning, heuristic and model-based filtering, MSA selection, and deduplication) with a partial-parameter CPT recipe that trains RS-LoRA adapters across the network together with the last eight transformer blocks and the embedding matrix, under layer-wise learning rates. At a matched 1B-token budget, CPT on AQL-curated data raises a four-benchmark Arabic mean by 3.51 points over CPT on raw web text, which yields no gain over the base model. In a controlled 5B-token comparison, AQL-Lite recovers 94% of the gain of full-parameter CPT (mean 73.19 vs. 73.58) in 52% of the wall-clock time and outperforms adapter-only baselines on every benchmark, and a component ablation shows that adapters, unfrozen blocks, and embedding training each contribute. Scaled to 40B MSA tokens and instruction-tuned on one million examples, the resulting 12B model scores 75.3 on the seven-benchmark Open Arabic LLM Leaderboard v2 (OALL v2) suite.

Our contributions are: • Arabic quality-first data pipeline. We introduce the AQL pipeline, a five-stage MSA corpus curation pipeline combining structural cleaning, heuristic filtering, MSA/dialect control, model-based quality and safety scoring, and exact/near deduplication, and show at a matched token budget that the curated data adds 3.51 points over raw web text. • Partial-parameter CPT. We propose AQL-Lite, a CPT recipe that combines RS-LoRA, selective upper-block unfreezing, embedding training, and layer-wise learning rates to approximate full-CPT gains at lower cost, and ablate its components. • Empirical evaluation for MSA adaptation. We compare AQL-Lite against full and adapter-only CPT in a controlled 5B-token setting, then evaluate the final 12B model on the OALL v2 suite, separating the contributions of CPT and instruction tuning.

We run controlled CPT experiments and one scale-up, all with the recipe of Section 3.2 : • Experiment 1 (5B tokens, recipe comparison): AQL-Lite against full CPT and adapter-only CPT on the same 5B-token subset, testing whether the recipe recovers most of the full-CPT gain at lower cost. • Ablations ( Section 4.1.2 ): a data ablation at a matched 1B-token budget, varying only the training data, and a component ablation at 5B tokens , varying only the recipe. • Experiment 2 (40B tokens, scale-up): the same recipe on 40B tokens of the MSA-only AQL corpus, followed by instruction tuning. We validate the recipe in a 5B-token controlled CPT setting, then scale CPT to 40B tokens (100% MSA), followed by 1M-example instruction tuning and deployment-time safety filtering.

We evaluate all checkpoints on four Arabic benchmarks: ArabicMMLU Koto et al. (2024) , AlGhafa Almazrouei et al. (2023) , AraTrust Alghamdi et al. (2025) , and Arabic EXAMS Hardalov et al. AQL-Lite remains an efficiency–performance trade-off rather than a full replacement for full-weight continual pretraining: in the controlled 5B-token experiment it recovers 94% of the full-CPT gain but does not match Full CPT on every benchmark. The main 40B-token scale-up uses a 100% MSA policy, which strengthens standardized Arabic performance but underrepresents dialectal Arabic, code-switching, and region-specific language use; the model should not be assumed to handle dialects well. Several choices are not fully ablated. The number of unfrozen blocks ( N = 8 N=8 ) was not tuned, the layer-wise learning-rate schedule is not ablated separately from the other components, and the data ablation applies Stages 3–5 jointly. All results come from single training runs, so differences below about one point should not be over-interpreted. We have not yet measured n n -gram overlap between our training data and the benchmarks, or the effect of CPT on English capabilities; both are planned for a future version. We also did not run full CPT at 40B tokens, so the efficiency comparison with full CPT is validated only at the 5B-token scale. Our efficiency comparison counts CPT wall-clock time only; it excludes the cost of running the Stage 3 and Stage 4 classifiers over the corpus and the cost of instruction tuning. As discussed in Section 6 , our benchmarks also cannot distinguish new knowledge from re-alignment of knowledge the base model already has.

Our evaluation is based on automatic benchmarks and a head-to-head comparison in which the comparison rows are taken from a public leaderboard that uses a different evaluation protocol, rather than re-run by us. The MSA classifier’s 99.96% accuracy is measured in-domain; such a high value may partly reflect annotation artifacts or near-duplicates shared between the training and validation splits, and an out-of-domain check on dialect identification data such as MADAR Bouamor et al. (2018) or NADI Abdul-Mageed et al. (2020) is needed to confirm it. The Stage 2 requirement of at least 70% Arabic characters likely removes technical and code-switched MSA, such as programming tutorials and scientific text with Latin-script terms, which may limit the model on technical and coding prompts. The evaluation may also not capture all dimensions of Arabic instruction-following, dialect robustness, factual reliability, or deployment safety. Finally, despite corpus filtering, safety instruction tuning, and an inference-time safety classifier, the model may still hallucinate, reflect biases from web data, or fail under adversarial prompting, especially in high-stakes domains.

AQL-Lite couples a quality-first curation pipeline (structural cleaning, heuristic and model-based filtering, MSA selection, and deduplication) with a partial-parameter CPT recipe that trains RS-LoRA adapters across the network together with the last eight transformer blocks and the embedding matrix, under layer-wise learning rates. At a matched 1B-token budget, CPT on AQL-curated data raises a four-benchmark Arabic mean by 3.51 points over CPT on raw web text, which yields no gain over the base model. In a controlled 5B-token comparison, AQL-Lite recovers 94% of the gain of full-parameter CPT (mean 73.19 vs. 73.58) in 52% of the wall-clock time and outperforms adapter-only baselines on every benchmark, and a component ablation shows that adapters, unfrozen blocks, and embedding training each contribute. Scaled to 40B MSA tokens and instruction-tuned on one million examples, the resulting 12B model scores 75.3 on the seven-benchmark Open Arabic LLM Leaderboard v2 (OALL v2) suite.

Our contributions are: • Arabic quality-first data pipeline. We introduce the AQL pipeline, a five-stage MSA corpus curation pipeline combining structural cleaning, heuristic filtering, MSA/dialect control, model-based quality and safety scoring, and exact/near deduplication, and show at a matched token budget that the curated data adds 3.51 points over raw web text. • Partial-parameter CPT. We propose AQL-Lite, a CPT recipe that combines RS-LoRA, selective upper-block unfreezing, embedding training, and layer-wise learning rates to approximate full-CPT gains at lower cost, and ablate its components. • Empirical evaluation for MSA adaptation. We compare AQL-Lite against full and adapter-only CPT in a controlled 5B-token setting, then evaluate the final 12B model on the OALL v2 suite, separating the contributions of CPT and instruction tuning.

We run controlled CPT experiments and one scale-up, all with the recipe of Section 3.2 : • Experiment 1 (5B tokens, recipe comparison): AQL-Lite against full CPT and adapter-only CPT on the same 5B-token subset, testing whether the recipe recovers most of the full-CPT gain at lower cost. • Ablations ( Section 4.1.2 ): a data ablation at a matched 1B-token budget, varying only the training data, and a component ablation at 5B tokens , varying only the recipe. • Experiment 2 (40B tokens, scale-up): the same recipe on 40B tokens of the MSA-only AQL corpus, followed by instruction tuning. We validate the recipe in a 5B-token controlled CPT setting, then scale CPT to 40B tokens (100% MSA), followed by 1M-example instruction tuning and deployment-time safety filtering.

We evaluate all checkpoints on four Arabic benchmarks: ArabicMMLU Koto et al. (2024) , AlGhafa Almazrouei et al. (2023) , AraTrust Alghamdi et al. (2025) , and Arabic EXAMS Hardalov et al. AQL-Lite remains an efficiency–performance trade-off rather than a full replacement for full-weight continual pretraining: in the controlled 5B-token experiment it recovers 94% of the full-CPT gain but does not match Full CPT on every benchmark. The main 40B-token scale-up uses a 100% MSA policy, which strengthens standardized Arabic performance but underrepresents dialectal Arabic, code-switching, and region-specific language use; the model should not be assumed to handle dialects well. Several choices are not fully ablated. The number of unfrozen blocks ( N = 8 N=8 ) was not tuned, the layer-wise learning-rate schedule is not ablated separately from the other components, and the data ablation applies Stages 3–5 jointly. All results come from single training runs, so differences below about one point should not be over-interpreted. We have not yet measured n n -gram overlap between our training data and the benchmarks, or the effect of CPT on English capabilities; both are planned for a future version. We also did not run full CPT at 40B tokens, so the efficiency comparison with full CPT is validated only at the 5B-token scale. Our efficiency comparison counts CPT wall-clock time only; it excludes the cost of running the Stage 3 and Stage 4 classifiers over the corpus and the cost of instruction tuning. As discussed in Section 6 , our benchmarks also cannot distinguish new knowledge from re-alignment of knowledge the base model already has.

Our evaluation is based on automatic benchmarks and a head-to-head comparison in which the comparison rows are taken from a public leaderboard that uses a different evaluation protocol, rather than re-run by us. The MSA classifier’s 99.96% accuracy is measured in-domain; such a high value may partly reflect annotation artifacts or near-duplicates shared between the training and validation splits, and an out-of-domain check on dialect identification data such as MADAR Bouamor et al. (2018) or NADI Abdul-Mageed et al. (2020) is needed to confirm it. The Stage 2 requirement of at least 70% Arabic characters likely removes technical and code-switched MSA, such as programming tutorials and scientific text with Latin-script terms, which may limit the model on technical and coding prompts. The evaluation may also not capture all dimensions of Arabic instruction-following, dialect robustness, factual reliability, or deployment safety. Finally, despite corpus filtering, safety instruction tuning, and an inference-time safety classifier, the model may still hallucinate, reflect biases from web data, or fail under adversarial prompting, especially in high-stakes domains.
